title: Redis Cloud architecture
summary: The subscription-to-database hierarchy, what each plan — Free and Paid Essentials, Essentials with Redis Flex, and Pro — includes and caps, and the availability story per tier from single-zone replication to multi-region Active-Active.

blocks.body:
Redis Cloud is a fully managed database service: you provision subscriptions and databases, and Redis operates the clusters, failover, patching, and maintenance underneath. Everything an operator decides starts from one mental model — an **account** contains **subscriptions**, and each **subscription** contains **databases** — plus a clear picture of what each subscription plan includes. This lesson walks that hierarchy top to bottom, because most architecture-domain exam questions are really asking: *which plan supports this capability, and what does it cost in limits or memory?*

## The hierarchy: account, subscription, database

An account is your tenant in the Redis Cloud console (cloud.redis.io). It owns team members, payment methods, and API keys. Within the account, a **subscription** is the commercial and deployment envelope: it fixes the cloud vendor (AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure), the region, and for Pro the dedicated deployment structure and Redis major version. A **database** is the actual Redis endpoint your clients connect to, with its own memory limit, throughput, modules, and security settings.

The shape differs by plan family:

- **Redis Cloud Essentials** subscriptions are built around a single database at a fixed monthly price. The plan you pick is the database's size and limit sheet; you choose vendor and region when you create the database itself.
- **Redis Cloud Pro** subscriptions are a shared envelope holding many databases, billed hourly on capacity. Pro deploys into Redis-managed dedicated VPCs, and the subscription carries settings that apply to its databases — including which Redis major version they run and where maintenance windows fall.

A free plan exists too: **Free Redis Cloud Essentials**. It gives one 30 MB database per account, for learning and prototyping. If the account already has a free database, you must delete it or upgrade it to a paid plan before creating a new one, and a free database left inactive long enough is removed (Redis support documents deletion after 14 days of inactivity) — so a free tier is never a storage home.

## Plans and their hard limits

The official comparison — memorize the tiers as Free Essentials / Paid Essentials / Essentials with Redis Flex / Pro — comes down to four columns:

| Capability | Free Essentials | Paid Essentials | Essentials + Redis Flex | Pro |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory | 30 MB | 250 MB - 12 GB | 1 - 100 GB | Up to 50 TB |
| Connections | 30 | 256 - 10,000 | 1,024 - 10,000 | No fixed database-level cap |
| REST API | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Replication / auto-failover | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Encryption at rest, private connectivity | No | No | No | Yes |
| Active-Active | No | No | No | Yes |

Three exam-visible asymmetries hide in that table. First, the **REST API is unavailable on free plans** — any automation question that starts with a free subscription has the wrong plan. Second, **backups through the console are a paid feature**: Pro and paid Essentials can back up and export; free plans cannot. Third, **encryption at rest and private connectivity are Pro-only**, so a requirement for either names Pro immediately.

**Essentials with Redis Flex** is a pricing/architecture variant of paid Essentials, not a separate product line: the database uses a RAM-plus-SSD tiered architecture in which all key names live in RAM while less-recent values spill to SSD. It suits datasets where the working set is much smaller than the full dataset, keys are small relative to values, and recent data is hottest — the cases with a high RAM hit rate. Flex trades single-digit-millisecond latency on warm data for far lower cost per gigabyte; if every access must be sub-millisecond, stay on RAM. Flex is available on Pro as well.

Pro plans come in pay-as-you-go and **annual** flavors. Annual Pro keeps the same feature set but lowers the price and adds Premium support, with the commitment applying across all of the account's workloads, providers, and regions.

## Regions and availability zones

Every database lands on a cloud vendor and region. Essentials databases choose theirs at creation; Pro subscriptions fix vendor and region for all databases in the subscription. Region choice is a latency and compliance decision — put the database next to the compute that queries it.

High availability then layers on top:

- **None** — a single copy, no replication. Cheapest, and the only option that risks data loss on any failure.
- **Single-zone** — a primary plus a replica in the same zone; the replica is promoted automatically if the primary fails (auto-failover on paid Essentials and Pro).
- **Multi-zone** — primary and replicas spread across availability zones, so the database survives the loss of an entire zone.

Zone-aware replication spreads primaries and replicas across zones, which is what lifts Pro deployments to high-availability SLAs: multi-zone Active-Active regions with three or more zones target 99.999% availability, while regions with fewer zones settle at 99.99% — and a deployment spanning both inherits the *weaker* number.

## Active-Active: the Pro geo-distribution story

**Active-Active** is the Pro-only geo-distribution capability. An Active-Active subscription defines up to 10 regions and holds up to 10 databases; every region hosts a full read-write copy of each database. Copies synchronize with conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), so writes in every region succeed locally and conflicts resolve deterministically — eventual consistency between regions, not blocking cross-region writes.

Each regional copy has its own endpoint; point each application at the nearest one for local latency. Know the operational costs: Active-Active requires replication to be on, and both replication and Active-Active synchronization double memory consumption, cumulatively up to **4x the data size**; eviction begins at **80% of the memory limit** rather than 100%; and there is no built-in failover of client connections across regions — surviving a whole-region outage needs a network-, proxy-, client-, or application-level routing strategy that you implement.

Where only one region is active and a second holds a read-only copy, the current Redis Cloud term is **Active-Passive** — it appears as a Durability setting linking a target database. Do not confuse it with Active-Active: passive copies are for recovery, not local writes.

## Choosing a tier: the decision shape

Exam scenarios compress to three questions. How much data? Under ~12 GB with modest throughput is Essentials territory; hundreds of gigabytes on a budget fits Flex; anything needing 50 TB-scale, clustering, or no fixed connection ceiling is Pro. Which capabilities? Active-Active, encryption at rest, private connectivity, Multi-AZ, configurable backup cadence — Pro only; replication and auto-failover need at least paid Essentials; the REST API needs anything but free. What availability target? None for throwaway work, single-zone for dev, multi-zone or Active-Active for production.

## Exam takeaways

- The hierarchy is account -> subscriptions -> databases; Essentials is one database per fixed-price plan, Pro is many databases in a dedicated-VPC subscription billed hourly.
- Tier names: Free Redis Cloud Essentials (30 MB, 30 connections, no REST API, no console backups), Paid Essentials (250 MB-12 GB, replication + auto-failover), Essentials with Redis Flex (1-100 GB, RAM+SSD tiering), Pro (up to 50 TB, no fixed connection cap).
- Pro-only capabilities: Active-Active, encryption at rest, private connectivity, Multi-AZ, Redis Flex on Pro, annual plans with Premium support.
- HA options are None / Single-Zone / Multi-Zone; multi-zone (three or more AZs) Active-Active targets 99.999%, fewer zones 99.99%, and a mixed deployment takes the lower figure.
- Active-Active: Pro, max 10 regions and 10 databases, CRDT eventual consistency, per-region endpoints, up to 4x memory, eviction at 80%, no built-in client failover.
- Active-Passive is the current Redis Cloud term for a linked read-only copy; free databases idle long enough are deleted (14 days per Redis support).
